title: Which famous documents are genuine?

lead.text: The documents divide cleanly by provenance. Those released from government files, such as the 1947 Twining memorandum, the Roswell press release and the 1953 Robertson Panel report, are genuine records of what officials wrote; the Majestic-12 papers arrived, by their recipients' account, as an anonymous roll of film, and the FBI says an Air Force investigation found the memo it received to be a fake; the Wilson-Davis notes surfaced from private papers, their author vouches for them and their subject denies the meeting.

answer.text: Twining's memorandum of 23 September 1947, signed as commander of Air Materiel Command, states that the phenomenon reported is something real and not visionary or fictitious, and asks that the objects be considered possibly of domestic origin, from a high security project unknown to Air Force intelligence.

The CIA's Robertson Panel of January 1953 recommended a programme of public education and debunking to strip UFOs of their aura of mystery and the monitoring of civilian UFO groups, and, according to the CIA's own historian, the CIA then forbade any mention that it had sponsored the panel.

According to NARA, the only document in its custody bearing the term MJ-12 is a 14 July 1954 memorandum from Robert Cutler to General Twining; NARA found it has no Top Secret register number, sits in a folder with no other MJ-12 material, lacks letterhead or watermark, and carries a marking the NSC FOIA office says was not used until the Nixon administration.

The Wilson-Davis notes are fifteen typed pages dated 16 October 2002, headed as Eric Davis's notes of a meeting with Vice Admiral Thomas Wilson, which record Wilson describing a 1997 refusal of access to a programme holding recovered material in a contractor's custody. They surfaced in 2019 from private papers, not from any government release.

A document can be genuine and still record only a belief: SIGN's 1948 Estimate of the Situation calling the objects interplanetary is known from the Condon Report, which says the Chief of Staff rejected it for lacking proof and copies were destroyed.

for.text: Eric Davis has confirmed to journalists that the notes are his, and said on a podcast in March 2026 that they are real and 100 percent accurate, that the circulating copy is a typewritten version of a handwritten one, and that it came from Edgar Mitchell's estate. He was an AAWSAP contract author of five of the 38 reference documents.

AARO's Volume I records a senior military officer describing a craft floating in a building with about 150 people working on it outside government, the structural allegation the Wilson-Davis notes describe; on the board's reading the refusal the notes describe matches the mechanism Grusch described under oath. That is an inference, not corroboration.

Friedman defended the core MJ-12 documents for a decade and produced fourteen examples of the typeface used in the Cutler-Twining memo to win $1,000 from Philip Klass; Robert and Ryan Wood's archive argues for the authenticity of substantial portions of the corpus.

The Estimate of the Situation is denied by Air Force representatives and Rep. Mendel Rivers, but the Condon Report, written under Air Force contract, records it; the board favours the contracted report on the ground that it was written with access to Air Force files, and says that weighing is its own inference.

The Roswell press release is a contemporaneous record: issued by 1st Lt. Walter Haut on 8 July 1947, it says the 509th's intelligence office "was fortunate enough to gain possession of a disc" through a local rancher and the sheriff's office.

against.text: The FBI states that in 1988 two of its offices received versions of a memo titled Operation Majestic-12 and that an Air Force investigation determined it to be a fake. Kevin Randle concluded the documents were not authentic, and Klass published a forensic critique of their anomalies in 1988.

On the board's reading the MJ-12 chain of custody disqualifies it: William Moore, one of the two recipients of the film, admitted at the 1989 MUFON symposium that he had cooperated with Air Force counterintelligence and knowingly passed false information to Paul Bennewitz, and the film's arrival falls inside that period. Friedman himself showed that one purported Hillenkoetter memo copied a published letter.

Thomas Wilson denies that the meeting took place and denies the substance attributed to him; Davis vouches for the text while saying he cannot confirm or deny that they met, and the DoD witnesses asked about the memo in 2022 said they were unaware of it.

The Wilson-Davis notes' route is itself second-hand and disputed: the notes carry Davis's own parenthesis that "Miller told Ed Mitchell who only told me in 1999"; one account has the pages leaving Mitchell's estate, another Kit Green's holdings, with Green not vouching for their contents.
The skeptic Brian Dunning calls the Wilson-Davis memo an obviously hoaxed document, and AARO attributes the reverse-engineering claim largely to circular reporting among believers.

Genuine documents do not always say what they are cited for: Twining's memorandum records that the lack of physical evidence in the form of crash-recovered exhibits constrained AMC's analysis, and the Estimate was rejected for lacking proof.

The twelve-page Immaculate Constellation report entered at the November 2024 hearing carries no author, classification marking or control number, and its first page credits the State Department with approving the public version, although the committee's index calls it a Pentagon report.

open: Who mailed the MJ-12 film to Shandera in December 1984?
How did the Cutler-Twining memo come to be in Record Group 341, and who placed it there?
Where did the Wilson-Davis notes go between 2002 and 2019, and did they reach the public from Mitchell's estate, from Kit Green's holdings, or both?
Does the handwritten version Davis mentions exist, and does it match the typed copy?
Who wrote the twelve-page report, and did it originate in the Pentagon as the Index of Documents describes it?

threads.text: The Wilson-Davis thread follows the notes outward, and most steps after them rest on reporting or inference rather than on a document. Davis is the author of record; the meeting is reported to have taken place at an EG&G facility in Las Vegas, a Tier 3 placement; Richard D'Amato's earlier Senate inquiry reached EG&G and stopped, and the view that a private-company cover-up was entirely feasible is attributed to him by George Knapp while his own statement treats the inquiry as closed; and AARO took the named companies' executives' denials on the record without naming a company or describing an inspection.
